extracted.intended_audience: students and professionals writing mathematics and computer-science papers, theses, books, programs, and technical documentation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and stylistic rules for preparing readable, well-organized mathematical and computer-science exposition (papers, theses, programs, user manuals, books). Emphasis on notation, proofs, sentence rhythm, typography, punctuation, and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate symbols in adjacent formulas with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Consider Sq, q p." Good: "Consider Sq, where q < p." Insert words between adjacent formula fragments so the prose reads smoothly and unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with a mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "xn - a has n distinct zeroes." Good: "The polynomial xn - a has n distinct zeroes."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical shorthand symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use symbols like '∴', '∵', '∀', '∃', etc., in ordinary mathematical exposition; replace them with words unless writing on logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except in works on logic, write out the corresponding words to avoid cryptic notation in running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preceding statement before theorem must be a complete sentence or end with a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentence immediately before a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or terminate with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fragments like "We now have the following" followed by "Theorem." Instead use a full lead-in such as "We can now prove the following result." and then state the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theorem statements self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained and not depend implicitly on assumptions in the preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate necessary hypotheses in the theorem itself so readers encountering the theorem directly still understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' to avoid passive voice, but use it responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'we' often helps avoid passive constructions; 'we' should mean 'you and me together', not a formal equivalent of 'I'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most technical writing avoid 'I' unless the author's persona matters. Use 'we' when it creates a cooperative dialog with the reader; disambiguate if multiple authors require it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect sentence rhythm and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a definite rhythm in sentences; read your prose aloud and revise if it does not flow smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose wording (e.g., 'merge patterns' vs 'merging patterns') to achieve correct cadence. Keep 'that' when it helps parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'assume' and 'suppose' normally with 'that'
rubrics_metrics.description: The verbs 'assume' and 'suppose' should usually be followed by 'that' to aid clarity unless another 'that' is nearby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid constructions like 'We have that x = ...' — prefer 'We have x = ...'. Avoid unnecessary padding like 'because of the fact that' unless needed for reader recuperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure and use parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentences to avoid monotony but use parallelism for parallel concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Prefer 'Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method.' Avoid repeating the same 'sticky' words in consecutive sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write homework-style sequences of formulas without commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid listing sequences of formulas with no running commentary; tie concepts together with explanatory prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add narrative to guide the reader through derivations and reasons, not just formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions/results twice in complementary ways
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving a definition or important concept, state it in two complementary forms to reinforce understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an informal description and a formal definition (examples given in §2). Define variables (at least informally) when first introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate the reader and keep the reader uppermost in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why results/definitions matter; consider what the reader knows and expects next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing others' work, let results speak or give reasons why they are interesting. When describing your own work, be humble and avoid superlatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write prose that survives skimming of formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers will skim or skip formulas on first reading; sentences should still read smoothly if formulas are replaced by placeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the textual flow does not rely entirely on detailed formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation and avoid reusing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use the same notation for two different things and be consistent about notation across the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose typographic conventions (lowercase for elements, uppercase for sets) and stick with them. Prefer consistent index naming so readers can visualize ranges easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts and avoid subscripted subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive subscripting; name set elements only when necessary to prevent cascading subscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use element notation to avoid layers of indices; avoid starting with X = {X1,...,Xn} if many subsets or elements will then require subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas and number important ones only
rubrics_metrics.description: Display significant formulas on a line by themselves and number the important ones (not every displayed formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give reference numbers to major formulas even if not immediately referenced to aid navigation; avoid numbering everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sentences so they parse left-to-right unambiguously
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be readable from left to right without temporary ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'Smith remarked in a paper about the scarcity of data' (ambiguous) and reorder to remove ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out small numbers used adjectivally
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out small numbers when used as adjectives, but not when referring to numerals as numbers (names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'The method requires 2 passes.' Good: 'Method 2 is illustrated in Fig. 1; it requires 17 passes. The count was increased by 2.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize labels like Theorem, Lemma, Algorithm in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize labels such as 'Theorem 1', 'Lemma 2', 'Algorithm 3' in titles and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent capitalization for such names throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe handy grammar maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch common grammar/style traps: sentence-ending prepositions, dangling participles, sentence fragments, pronoun agreement, unnecessary commas, split infinitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are general cautions; don't follow rigidly if an exception improves clarity or rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common misspellings and modern hyphenation changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of frequent misspellings by computer scientists and avoid outdated hyphenation (e.g., 'nonnegative', 'nonzero' are no longer hyphenated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spelling checkers and updated style references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'that' vs 'which' according to restrictive vs nonrestrictive usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'which' only when it is nonrestrictive (usually preceded by a comma) or in other appropriate cases; prefer 'that' when it sounds better for restrictive clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with phrasing to decide which reads better; avoid ambiguous use that forces reader parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation with displayed formulas and colons
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse colons before displayed equations; often the formula completes the sentence without a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lead-in is a full sentence then a colon is fine; otherwise omit extraneous colons. Be careful with punctuation around displayed material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-load your best paragraph and opening sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph and its first sentence should be your best; hooks help keep readers engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stale starts like 'An x is y.' Give context and motivation early to hook the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow conventional punctuation with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: By convention, commas and periods go inside quotation marks; other punctuation stays outside unless part of the quotation. Parenthetical punctuation must be logically correct on its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put a period inside parentheses iff the parenthesized clause is a full sentence. Ensure punctuation remains correct if the parenthesized text is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long noun-strings and unnecessary jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist long chains of nouns used as adjectives (noun clusters) and avoid jargon unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clearer phrasing and a nonspecialist's vocabulary when possible; long noun strings hinder readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with ellipses and spacing in formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Put commas before and after ellipses when appropriate; position dots at mid-level when between symbols like '+'; watch spacing around ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spacing and alignment matter: e.g., '(P1, . . . , Pn)' needs proper commas and vertical alignment for the dots in typeset math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid linebreaks inside formulas and psychologically bad breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not break lines awkwardly in the middle of formulas or leave final symbols isolated on a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typesetting tools (TeX nonbreaking constructs, tildes) to tie elements together and prevent bad breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between mathematical notation and programming notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematical notation in formal papers, not programming shorthand; e.g., prefer subscripts over program-style p[r] and 'xy' over '*' for multiplication in math texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve programming notation for code examples and use math-appropriate notation elsewhere for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment and signpost proofs and complex arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what's going on in proofs: give signposts, subgoals, and brief strategy comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'We demonstrate the second conclusion by contradiction' or 'There must be a witness...' guide readers and introduce helpful vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number displayed formulas sparingly (only important ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number only the most important displayed formulas rather than numbering everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraneous numbering distracts; number those you will reference or that are central to the exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous parentheses and nested parentheses when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many parentheses, especially nested ones, burden the reader; remove unnecessary pairs or use typographic conventions to clarify nesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler phrasing; if nested parentheses are unavoidable, typographers often use slightly larger outer parentheses for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typographic/notation conventions appropriate to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt conventions like boldface for vectors or arrows as appropriate to the intended readers, but don't overuse typographic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive fonts, all-caps, or boldface; those convey shouting or distraction. Let conventions aid readability, not dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraphing clear around displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: When using displayed equations, take care to make paragraph breaks and new paragraphs obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor paragraph signaling around displays confuses readers; use whitespace and clear lead-in/lead-out sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nonbreaking spaces to tie terms together
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nonbreaking spaces (e.g., TeX tilde) to prevent undesirable line breaks between related items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids final-symbol isolation and keeps phrases intact for reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with quotation marks and gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing quotation marks or cute constructions; too many quotes or gimmicks distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three cute things in quotes is usually too cute; use quotes only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checkers and watch common misspellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who are weak spellers should use spelling checkers; be aware of discipline-specific misspellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short list of often-misspelled words is provided; consult dictionaries and style guides for hyphenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize the use of subscripts to keep notation readable and avoid nested indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to refer to elements or use clearer notation rather than Pi, Pi_j style that creates cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols and notation when first used
rubrics_metrics.description: Define all variables and symbols (at least informally) when they first appear, or very near where they are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to define notation forces reader confusion; place definitions where they are most natural for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with verb tenses; choose present or sequential style
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use present tense throughout or adopt a sequential style (past/present/future markers); avoid mixing tenses awkwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential writing (e.g., 'We saw this before. We will see this later.') suits long papers; use words of duration for better effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' vs imperative vs first person deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternatives to 'we': imperative sentences or indicative statements can avoid both passive voice and the 'we' construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Replace x by 7 throughout.' instead of 'We can now prove the following result.' Use style that best serves clarity and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs when possible (avoid proof-by-contradiction if unnecessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction are often less clear to readers when a direct proof is available; favor direct arguments for exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct proofs tend to be more illuminating and sometimes avoid extraneous integer assumptions; use contradiction sparingly and only when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice and awkward passive constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor active constructions or other alternatives to passive voice to improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'It can be shown...' with 'A proof shows...' or similar active formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational signposts and transitions for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone with signposts, transitional paragraphs, and announced plan/parts makes proofs and papers more pleasant to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'We divide the proof into two parts...' or 'The operative word is zero.' help readers follow structure and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in phrasing mathematical relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exact wording to distinguish related but different properties (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' vs 'increasing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't conflate 'nonincreasing' with 'increasing'—specify exact quantifiers and indices to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization: spend time on structure; 'Do organize' and 'Do not distract'
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization is critical—material must be arranged to form a coherent plot, weaving branches and threads rather than just linear order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should devote significant effort to arranging material logically and avoid distracting notational or stylistic choices; use Roget's, encyclopedias, and good textbooks as models of complex organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything that helps communication is good; anything that hurts is bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an overarching test: prefer choices that help communication and avoid those that hurt it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many specific rules are subordinate to this guiding principle—if a stylistic exception aids communication, it is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value professional copy editors and typesetters
rubrics_metrics.description: When self-publishing or preparing books, remember the value of professionals (copy editors, designers) to improve readability and correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should still rewrite and polish but engage professionals for layout, punctuation consistency, and design choices that improve reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conservative with exclamation points and novelty devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be used sparingly—only for true exclamations or interjections—since they can distract and annoy readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Halmos suggested tricks (e.g., parenthetical '!') but general advice is to avoid overuse; similar conservatism applies to jokes and gimmicks: use them only when they will remain sensible on re-readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt consistent bibliographic/citation conventions helpful to novices
rubrics_metrics.description: In bibliographies, consider spelling out full journal names and preserving original forms to aid novices locating sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knuth's bibliography keeps mathematical formulas and full names to help inexperienced readers find references in libraries.
